title: Organised crime inside the state
summary: In dozens of countries the official who decides who gets raided is also taking money from someone who needs not to be. A trafficking or smuggling network rarely wants a law changed. What it wants is discretion: which warehouse is searched, which file moves, which extradition request is answered, which rival gets arrested. So it goes for the offices that hold that discretion — the interior ministry, which runs the police; customs and border posts; the prosecutor's office; the judges who sign warrants; and the appointments that fill all of those. Sometimes it reaches the top, and a president, a state governor or a military intelligence chief is named as part of the network itself. The approach is usually not a bag of cash from a stranger. It comes through family: Montenegro's former supreme court president is in prison for using her position to protect a cigarette and narcotics ring run by her son. It comes through campaign money, through a police commander who begins by keeping a share of seized cash, through a businessman who holds an honorary title and advises ministers. What the network gets is the state's enforcement machinery aimed at its competitors rather than at itself. Proven cases sit in 64 countries, and they are not only poor ones; police officers in several American cities have been convicted of guarding cocaine shipments or robbing dealers.
implications: The raid that was planned does not happen, or happens to the wrong people. A case file sits until the witnesses are gone. A rival trafficker is arrested and the protected one keeps the route, so the violence does not fall evenly — it falls on whoever is outside the arrangement, including police who refuse the money. People living there usually cannot see any of this; it surfaces through a foreign indictment, a decrypted phone or a car crash. Worth watching: who is handed the interior ministry, customs and judicial appointments, and whether officials named in foreign courts are promoted rather than removed.
uncertain: Many of the strongest entries rest on US indictments that have never been tried, because the accused stays at home, and a charge is not a finding. Where a court has ruled the dossier gives the verdict; the Venezuelan, Sinaloa and Haitian allegations remain untested, and one of them was publicly doubted by US intelligence analysts even as the administration asserted it.

title: China's long arm abroad
summary:
China's government works on other countries' politics mostly through people who are already inside them. The Chinese Communist Party keeps a body for this, the United Front Work Department, whose job is to build influence over Chinese communities abroad and over foreign elites, and on this map it rarely appears under its own name. What appears instead is a community association, a 'friendship' group, a property developer who gives to both main parties, a campaign treasurer, an aide in a governor's office. The posts targeted are local as often as national: a city council seat, a village chief, a parliamentary researcher's desk. Those are cheap to reach and they still decide things Beijing cares about — what a council says about Taiwan, who gets to see a legislator, whether a diaspora critic is left in peace.

A second route runs through police work. Chinese city police bureaus set up 'overseas service stations' used to press people wanted in China to go home, and in the Pacific, Chinese officers now work inside local forces on rotation. Money moves as well: a discretionary fund in the Solomon Islands prime minister's office, paid for by China, reached 39 of the country's 50 members of parliament.

The approach is made by someone the target already knows and trusts, which is the point of using go-betweens. A voter sees a generous donor or a busy community leader, not the consulate or the party office behind them.
implications: A council votes on a resolution about Taiwan and the wording came from somewhere else. A critic of Beijing living in your city gets calls and visits telling them to go home, and the local police have no file on it. A party nomination meeting fills up with bused-in voters. Where Chinese officers sit inside a national police force, the people being pressured cannot tell which officer is which. Worth watching: who funds and who runs a local candidate's campaign, whether a government publishes its security services' warnings, and whether policing agreements with China are put before parliament.
uncertain: Much of this record comes from security-service warnings, cancelled visas and press reports rather than court findings, and several prosecutions have failed: a former Canadian police officer was acquitted, with the verdict under appeal, and Britain dropped its case against a parliamentary researcher. Where the United Front is named, the dossier often does not establish that the person involved knew who they were working for. The report that Chinese spy chips were built into server motherboards was denied by the companies named and has not been substantiated.

title: Russia's networks in Europe and Africa
summary:
Russia runs two different operations, and they reach for different parts of a state. In parts of Africa it sells protection. Governments that took power by coup and then sent French, US or UN forces away need someone to guard the president and train the army, and the Russian defence ministry's Africa Corps, which took over most of this work from the Wagner Group after Yevgeny Prigozhin died in 2023, supplies the men. The deal is made leader to leader and signed as a defence agreement covering training, arms, intelligence sharing and port calls for Russian ships. Reporting links some of these deployments to gold, diamond and timber concessions, so the host pays partly in minerals.

In Europe the target is not the army but people already elected, or recently retired from office. The approach runs through party-to-party cooperation pacts signed in Moscow, board seats at Russian state energy companies, paid speeches and media projects, and through the Moscow Patriarchate, the Russian Orthodox Church, whose parishes abroad answer to a patriarch who backs the war in Ukraine. Germany's former chancellor Gerhard Schröder chaired the board of the state oil company Rosneft until 2022, which was lawful and openly declared; other arrangements are private contracts, and voters generally learn of them only after a raid, a leak or a trial. What Russia buys in both places is the same thing: a decision taken in its favour by someone the public chose, or cannot remove.
implications: Where Russian troops guard a president, the people who would normally be able to remove him matter less, because his safety no longer depends on them. Mining and timber rights signed as part of such an arrangement are rarely published, so a country's gold can leave without passing through its budget. In Europe, someone voting for a party has no way of knowing it has a funding or cooperation arrangement with a foreign ruling party. Worth watching: whether those party pacts are renewed or allowed to lapse, what the governments protected by Africa Corps hand over in return, and whether paid-speech cases ever reach a verdict.
uncertain: Much of this is untested. A Bulgarian court acquitted the pro-Russia figure charged with collecting state secrets for a Russian state think tank, and the German case against an AfD politician accused of taking money from the Voice of Europe network is unfinished. The link between troop deployments and mining concessions comes from reporting rather than published contracts, and troop numbers in Africa are estimates by analysts and UN monitors.

title: Governments buying officials in other countries

In the 1970s the Korean Central Intelligence Agency and businessman Tongsun Park paid US congressmen ('Koreagate'); the House Fraser subcommittee (1978) also examined the KCIA's use of Sun Myung Moon's organisations.
The Russkiy Mir Foundation (2007) and the Voice of Europe network, sanctioned by the Czech government in March 2024 for paying European politicians.

summary: Several governments are at work right now trying to buy the loyalty of officials in other countries, and courts and public inquiries keep turning up pieces of it. What the sponsoring state usually wants is one decision: an arms sale approved, a sanctions listing dropped, an extradition refused, a friendlier candidate in office. So it goes for whoever controls that decision rather than for a government as a whole: the legislative committee that signs off on weapons and aid, the interior ministry that runs the police, the party founder who nominates the prime minister. The approach generally comes through the same doors as ordinary lobbying, as a consulting contract, donations handed over by an intermediary, a community association, paid travel, or staff and money at election time. A proxy usually makes the offer, so the official who takes it may not know which government is behind it, and voters almost never can. Not all of it is money. United Nations experts report that Rwanda commands the armed group M23 and runs a parallel administration in the part of eastern Congo it holds, and Uganda sent special forces into Juba to guard South Sudan's president at a moment when his government was detaining ministers allied with his main rival. What the sponsor gets is a standing voice inside another country's decisions. The cost lands on people who elected one government and get another government's priorities.
uncertain: Much of this is reported but never tested: the Canadian inquiry found that proxies of India's government may have funded politicians without naming any, and the parliamentarians described as witting participants in interference were never identified. Several cases ended with no finding either way, through an acquittal, a pardon before trial and a dismissal, so the record does not settle what was or was not done. Where a state is said to direct an armed group, a hack or a killing, that state denies it.

implications: The decision goes the other way than it would have. A weapons shipment is cleared, a prosecution of a foreign government's suspects is quietly settled, a police force is trained abroad and brings those methods home, or a candidate wins on money nobody can trace. Registration rules are what make any of this visible, and most of the prosecutions here turned on someone failing to register as a foreign agent. Worth watching are consulting contracts with foreign state companies, sudden clusters of donations, officials pressing one country's line on arms, sanctions or extraditions, and how the cases end, since several closed by pardon or dismissal rather than by a verdict.

title: Governments inside companies
summary: Governments sit inside private companies right now, in several different ways at once, and most of a company's customers cannot tell. What a state wants from a firm varies: the data passing through it, a say in its decisions, its profits, or a place in its supply chain. That decides which firms get the attention. Telecom carriers, software suppliers and makers of encryption equipment are worth most, because one position inside them reaches every customer at once — the CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned a Swiss cipher firm that sold machines to more than 120 governments, and read those governments' traffic for decades before it became public. The methods run from the legal to the covert. China's company law requires a firm with three or more Communist Party members to set up a party organisation inside it, and state funds take board seats. Russia puts foreign-owned businesses under 'temporary management' by decree and installs new managers. Turkey's trustee fund holds companies it seized as linked to a religious movement. Iran's Revolutionary Guards own an industrial group outright through their engineering arm. North Korea places its own programmers in foreign firms under stolen identities and collects their wages. Chinese state hackers have sat in carriers' core networks, including the systems used for lawful wiretaps. Shareholders, subscribers and app users are rarely told which, if any, of this applies to them.
implications: When a state is inside a company, decisions that look commercial are not. A call record or a message can be read without a warrant or a court. A foreign owner's factory changes hands without a law being passed, and the shares in it become worthless. A supplier's routine software update carries someone else's code into thousands of its customers. Nobody is told at the time. Things to watch: seizures of foreign-owned firms under emergency management rules, remote staff whose identity cannot be verified, and who sits on the board of the company that runs the phone network or the power grid.
uncertain: Several entries are attributions rather than findings: the antivirus maker denies the security service ties the US government cites, and the payments executive named as a Russian intelligence asset has fled and never been tried. The Philippine grid stake and the German espionage case were raised by legislators and prosecutors but are not settled. Party committees are required by Chinese law, but what any particular one decides inside a firm is not public.

title: Foreign money inside Europe's parliaments
summary:
Foreign money inside Europe's assemblies is a set of live criminal cases, not a closed chapter. The target is rarely a national government. It is a parliament, and inside it a few members who sit in the right place: a vice-president of the chamber, the chair of a human-rights subcommittee, the vice-chair of a delegation that handles one region. A member like that can table a resolution, soften a report, or make a speech that a foreign ministry will quote at home. No election has to be won and nobody has to be convinced except the members themselves.

The money normally arrives wrapped in something lawful. A Brussels human-rights charity run by a former member of the European Parliament is alleged to have passed on cash from Qatar and Morocco; that case, Qatargate, is still running after an appeal court allowed it to proceed. Elsewhere it is consultancy fees, a company invoice, football tickets and paid travel, or a long bank chain — leaked records showed about $2.9 billion moving through one Danish bank's Estonian branch, some of it reaching politicians who defended Azerbaijan at the Council of Europe's assembly of national MPs.

Small assemblies are favoured because their reports on elections and political prisoners carry weight abroad while almost nobody reads them at home. The members charged come from centre-right, socialist and nationalist parties alike, and the paying governments are not all of one kind either.
implications: An assembly's report on an election or on political prisoners comes out softer than the facts, and the government it concerns quotes it as a clean bill of health. A debate gets a speech nobody can trace to whoever paid for it. A committee set up to scrutinise a company hears from members who have taken its hospitality and travel. Things to watch: whether members have to declare outside income, gifts and trips; whether charities and consultancies used as channels must name their funders; and how long a parliament takes to lift immunity once prosecutors ask for it.
uncertain: Most of the central entries are charges, open investigations or lifted immunities rather than convictions: Qatargate is untried and those charged deny it, and the Huawei inquiry in Belgium has produced no verdict. The 2018 inquiry into Azerbaijani money at the Council of Europe's assembly reported strong suspicion and breaches of its own rules for most of the members it named, not proven bribery.

title: Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement
roles: Country that handed people over or closed schools
summary:
Turkey's government is still asking other governments to hand over people it links to the Gülen movement, and many of them agree. The movement, which calls itself Hizmet, is a religious network built around the preacher Fethullah Gülen; it ran schools, charities and businesses in dozens of countries. Since the failed coup of July 2016, which Ankara blames on it, Turkey treats it as a terrorist organisation and its teachers and school directors abroad as fugitives.

The approach is state to state and usually quiet. Turkey's foreign ministry asks a host government to close the local Gülen schools and transfer them to Maarif, a Turkish state school operator. It asks an interior ministry or intelligence service to detain named residents, then flown out on a chartered plane, sometimes before a court can intervene. Where a government will not help, Turkish intelligence has seized people itself. Alongside this runs the Diyanet, Turkey's state religious directorate, which employs imams as civil servants and runs mosques abroad; after the coup attempt it instructed them to gather information on Gülen followers and gave parliament reports covering 38 countries.

What Turkey gets is reach over its own diaspora; what the host government gets is Turkish goodwill, aid and investment, with no duty to explain the file it acted on. An older strand runs inward instead: the Grey Wolves, the youth wing of a Turkish nationalist party, whose ties to police and ministers surfaced in 1996 when a crash near Susurluk put an MP, a police chief and a wanted gunman in the same car.
implications: A teacher or a recognised refugee living legally in another country can be picked up and flown to Turkey on a request the host government never publishes, with no hearing worth the name. Parents find the school closed and reopened under new management, with their children's records handed over with the building. Worshippers at a mosque abroad may not know their imam is a civil servant of another state who has been asked to report names. Worth watching: whether a host government publishes the legal basis for a handover, whether its own courts rule against it afterwards, and who employs the imams at local Turkish mosques.
uncertain: Most Gülen-related verdicts in Turkey come from courts whose own judges were replaced in the purge, and the movement's role in the 2016 coup attempt has not been tested by any court outside Turkey. Several handovers are documented only through statements by host officials, with no published legal basis; the European Court of Human Rights found one set of transfers unlawful. Belonging to the movement is lawful in most of the countries involved.

title: Churches and movements placing members in the state
summary: Members of religious movements sit in cabinets, parliaments and presidencies across much of the world, almost always lawfully, while in a smaller set of countries the state is breaking such movements up. A movement generally wants two things from government: law and schooling that match its teaching, and protection for its own institutions and money. It works on the ruling party rather than the state directly, because a party needs volunteers, donations and reliable votes, and a church can supply all three at once. The usual method is simply to supply people. Members stand as candidates, graduates are placed in the police and the courts, a cross-party caucus votes as a bloc on the questions its churches care about, and a church signs its followers up as party members in bulk. In India, 38 of the 53 ministers in one recent government came up through the RSS, a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation whose political wing grew into the governing party. Turkey shows the same machinery running backwards: after the 2016 coup attempt the government blamed a religious network whose graduates had reached the police and the judiciary, and dismissed public employees by the tens of thousands. Belonging to a church while holding office is not wrongdoing. The difficulty begins when a movement's own leaders, rather than voters or the civil service, decide who rises and what they do once there.
uncertain: Most of these movements do not publish membership rolls, so many entries rest on press reporting and are marked probable or possible, and some are denied, as Opus Dei denies that one former US attorney general was a member. Turkey's attribution of the 2016 coup attempt to the Gulen movement comes from its own courts and was denied by the defendants. Where a figure was raised in a movement rather than enrolled in it, the record shows upbringing, not instruction.

implications: Policy moves in ways nobody voted on directly: a school curriculum rewritten, a bill on marriage or reproduction killed in committee, a ministry staffed out of one congregation's address book. Where the state turns on a movement instead, a teacher or a police officer loses their job over who they prayed with, and a judiciary can lose thousands of judges in a day, which stalls every case waiting in front of them. Things to watch: mass sign-ups of followers as party members, churches lending campaign volunteers, caucuses that vote as a bloc, and dismissals justified by membership alone rather than by anything the person did.

title: Religious nationalism in power
summary: These movements are legal, open and popular, and their people reach office by winning elections, which makes this the least hidden arrangement on the map. What they want is not a secret decision but ordinary government power applied to religion: a constitution rewritten, rules on conversion and marriage, school curricula, official honours for shrines and monks, one legal code in a country that has several. The offices that matter are therefore the cabinet itself, the ministries of religion and education, and the task forces and committees that draft such laws. The route in is membership. A movement trains organisers for decades and then supplies them to a party: India's prime minister worked for years as a full-time organiser of the Hindu nationalist volunteer body whose political wing grew into his party, and a news site's count put 38 of the 53 ministers in his second government as having the same background. In Japan a nationalist lobby and the political arm of the shrine association each run a league of members of parliament, and press counts have placed most of a cabinet in one or both. Buddhist monks' groups in Sri Lanka and Myanmar have been given a presidential task force and a state honour, and four laws on conversion, marriage and birth spacing were drafted from texts one of them proposed. Hizb ut-Tahrir works the other way, recruiting army officers from outside, and is banned in several countries.
implications: When a cabinet and a movement are largely the same people, the movement's aims can arrive as government policy without any public argument about the movement itself. A marriage or conversion law appears already drafted. A body set up to reform the law is chaired by the leader of a group accused of stirring religious violence. Minorities feel it first, in what can be taught, who may marry whom, whether a complaint is taken up. Membership lists are often unpublished, so outsiders depend on reporters' counts. Watch who drafts laws on religion and family, and whether courts can still undo political favours.
uncertain: The membership counts come from journalists and researchers, not from the organisations, which publish no rolls; the RSS keeps none. Belonging to a lawful movement is not itself wrongdoing, and the dossier records no finding against the ministers counted. Whether membership changed any particular decision is not established.

title: Governments that export religion
roles: Where the mosques or churches are
summary:
Several governments pay for, staff or control places of worship in other countries, and the host states are now unpicking those ties. Turkey's Diyanet, its state directorate of religious affairs, employs imams as civil servants and runs over 2,000 mosques abroad through national branches. Saudi Arabia worked through the Muslim World League, a missionary body it funds. Russia's reach runs through the Moscow Patriarchate — the Russian Orthodox Church — whose patriarch backs the war in Ukraine.

What a sponsoring state gets is a standing relationship with its own emigrants and their children: it picks the preacher, shapes the teaching, pays bills a congregation cannot meet, and has somewhere to speak from that is not an embassy. Sometimes it asks for more. After the 2016 coup attempt in Turkey, the Diyanet instructed its imams abroad to collect information on followers of the Gülen movement, and handed the Turkish parliament intelligence reports drawn from dozens of countries.

Host governments answer with administrative tools rather than criminal law: a ban on foreign funding of religious bodies, a residence permit not renewed, an amendment to a church statute. Belgium took back the Great Mosque of Brussels, which it had lent to Saudi Arabia rent-free in 1967 on a 99-year lease, then blocked the replacement management body after its security service found members tied to foreign intelligence. The sponsoring state tends to call this an attack on religion, as Turkey did when Austria reviewed its imams' permits.

A congregation in the middle of it usually cannot tell where the money or the instructions come from.
implications: The imam or priest at your mosque or parish is chosen, paid and recalled by a government abroad, and what is said from the pulpit follows that government's politics rather than the congregation's. In the Turkish case, people who simply attended a mosque had their names and opinions reported home. When a host state cuts off the foreign money, the building and the clergy still have to be paid for, and often nobody has arranged how. Worth watching: who employs the clergy and who pays them, whether a congregation can choose its own, and how a ban gets applied parish by parish.
uncertain: The German investigation into Diyanet imams suspected of informing on Gülen supporters ended without spying being proved, and the funding cuts and permit reviews that followed were administrative decisions, not findings of a crime. The Dutch parliamentary inquiry documented Gulf money and influence over teaching and the choice of imams, but did not establish that any government directed it. How far Moscow Patriarchate parishes abroad take instruction from Moscow, as against sharing its position, is not settled on this record.

title: Consultants and lobbyists inside the ministries
summary:
Private advisers now sit inside governments as a matter of routine, and the part of the state they are hired into is usually the part that writes rules or spends money: a treasury's tax-policy team, a revenue service, a prime minister's delivery unit, a procurement office. The firms are accountancies, management consultancies, law and public-relations firms, and single companies lobbying for themselves. Some are paid by the government. Some are paid by a foundation or a wealthy donor and placed in a ministry at no charge, which keeps them off the public payroll and out of the procurement record altogether.

The arrangement is lawful and the contract is often public; the work is not. A firm can be seconded to help draft a tax law and then sell clients advice on the law it helped write. A consultancy can be hired to reorganise a tax service and cut the unit that produced a large share of its revenue, which is what South Africa's Zondo Commission into state capture found Bain & Company did. A company's lobbyist can reach a minister by text message, outside the diary and outside the freedom-of-information file.

What the outside firm gets is the inside of a decision before anyone else, and often the next contract. What the government gets is speed and expertise it says it does not have. The record generally surfaces years later through a leak, a parliamentary inquiry or a prosecution, and firms that pay penalties in one country usually keep working in the others.
implications: The tax rule that would have closed a loophole is drafted with help from people who sell advice on loopholes, so it arrives with the gap already in it. The investigators who were examining large taxpayers are reorganised out of their jobs. A licence or a market opens for one company because a minister took its calls, and its competitors never knew there was a conversation to join. Worth watching: which outside advisers sit in your government's central offices, who is paying them, whether ministers' messages with companies are kept as public records, and whether a firm barred from contracts stays barred.
uncertain: Several of these inquiries found no rule broken: UK reviews cleared David Cameron over his lobbying for Greensill Capital, and Bain denies 'wilfully' helping to capture South Africa's revenue service. Where messages were deleted or never released, what was actually agreed is not established. The French tax-fraud inquiry into McKinsey has produced a seizure but no verdict.

title: Global firms buying governments
summary: The largest sums on this map come from companies paying the people who run governments, and much of it is still moving through courts. A firm wants a specific thing: a construction contract, an oil cargo on good terms, a mining licence, a law that rescues a loss-making power plant. So it goes for whoever decides that one thing, which means the chief executive of the state oil company, the speaker who controls which bills reach a vote, or the finance minister who signs the state guarantee. The payment rarely looks like a payment. Odebrecht, a Brazilian builder, ran a department whose job was bribery and admitted paying 788 million dollars across a dozen countries; elsewhere the money arrives as a consulting fee, a commission of a few cents on each barrel traded, jobs and contracts for a legislator's associates, or posts for officials' relatives. Sometimes a company reaches for the appointment itself: South Africa's deputy finance minister says the Gupta brothers, businessmen close to the president, offered him the finance ministry, which the family denies. What the firm gets is the contract, and often the terms it helped write. The cost is carried by people who never see the transaction, because the bribe sits inside the price of the road, the fuel or the electricity, and because public money is sometimes spent rescuing the payer.
implications: The contract goes to the firm that paid rather than the firm that bid best, and at a price with the bribe built into it. The law that follows protects the payer, as with the Ohio legislation that rescued a power company's nuclear plants at the public's expense and sent the state House speaker to prison. These cases also tend to surface in foreign courts, in the United States or Switzerland, rather than where the officials were paid, so a country can go years without learning what happened to its own procurement. Worth watching: how the appeals go, and whether any money returns to the country whose officials were bought.
uncertain: Several matters here are unresolved, with appeals pending, a trial under way by video link from asylum, and charges denied, including by the Indian conglomerate accused in New York. One former Brazilian president's convictions were annulled because the court that tried him lacked jurisdiction, which is a ruling about the court rather than a finding that nothing happened. Some of the strongest-sounding detail comes from executives negotiating plea deals and has not been tested against them in court.

title: Industries inside their regulators
summary: The bodies meant to check an industry very often have that industry's people inside them, or working on their rules. What a company wants here is the decision made before anyone outside knows a decision is being made: the safety certificate, the licence, the wording of a clause, the contract. So the target is not the floor vote but the places upstream of it — the agency that certifies, the committee that drafts, the ministry that buys, and in the largest cases the presidency of an international negotiation. Counting names on the official participant lists, a campaign coalition found at least 2,456 fossil-fuel lobbyists accredited to the UN climate talks in Dubai, whose president also ran the host state's oil company. The routes in are mundane and mostly lawful. Staff move between a regulator and the firms it oversees. A regulator delegates its own safety checks to company employees, as US aviation regulators still do with the country's largest plane maker. Model bills written by industry-funded groups are introduced by legislators who did not write them; one newspaper investigation found roughly 10,000 such bills in US statehouses, more than 4,000 of them to the benefit of industry. Where it is not lawful it is bribery, and construction, software and consulting firms have admitted paying officials for contracts and for laws. The public normally learns which it was from a leak, a lawsuit or a public inquiry, years later.
implications: The rule that would have cost money is not written, or is written the way the industry asked. A safety check is signed off by the company being checked, and a plane, a building or a drug stays in use longer than it should. A contract goes to the firm that paid rather than the one that bid best, and the public covers the difference. None of it is visible at the moment of decision. Watch for company staff performing a regulator's inspections, officials moving straight into the industry they regulated, identical bills appearing in many legislatures, and industry delegates inside international talks.
uncertain: Several of the largest matters here are charges rather than verdicts: the Israeli bribery trial over telecoms decisions is unfinished and the defendant denies the charges, and the Panamanian and Ukrainian cases are in progress. The COP28 president called the reporting on his oil-deal talking points false. Where a firm has admitted bribery in a US settlement, the admission covers the firm, not every official named alongside it.

title: Criminal money inside banks and firms
summary:
Criminal organisations today do not only pay off banks and companies; in much of this record they own them, staff them, or work from a desk inside them. What they need is not secrecy but its opposite: an invoice, a payroll, an audited account, a contract with the state. Money that arrives as bus-fare revenue, a fuel delivery, a construction payment or a client's deposit stops looking like crime, and the business goes on serving ordinary customers who know nothing about it.

So the parts of a firm they go for are the ones that touch money or movement. Bank branches that take cash from exchange houses or non-resident clients. Terminal staff and IT contractors at container ports, who can hand over the codes that release a container from the port's own system. Customs desks and fuel-import chains. Petrol stations, ethanol plants, investment funds, casinos and junket operators. In São Paulo, prosecutors charge that Brazil's largest criminal organisation laundered money through two bus companies carrying the city's passengers, one of them running about 1,200 buses.

The approach is usually made to a mid-level employee rather than a boss — a port worker, a teller, a compliance officer — because that is where the access sits and the salary is small. And the usual ending is a fine paid by the company with nobody charged, which is why the same channel reopens under new names, as other Baltic banks did after Danske Bank's single Estonian branch was found to have moved roughly 200 billion euros of non-resident money.
implications: The bus you ride, the petrol station on the corner and the firm rebuilding after an earthquake may be where someone's drug money is being cleaned, and the passengers and workers carry that risk without being told. A container leaves a port because a worker sold a release code, so the seizure that should have happened does not. The company pays a fine out of revenue, no individual is named, and the service carries on. Worth watching: actions against firms that hold public contracts, ports and free zones where staff are arrested, and settlements in which nobody is named.
uncertain: Many of the largest entries are prosecutors' allegations or sanctions designations rather than verdicts, and a designation is an executive act, not a court's finding. Some collapse: the offshore law firm at the centre of the Panama Papers saw its founders and others acquitted in 2024, the judge citing insufficient and improperly gathered evidence. Figures for amounts laundered, whether through bank branches, funds or crypto mixers, come from investigators and blockchain analysis and are estimates rather than settled sums.

title: Companies inside other companies
summary:
Governments are now intervening in deals where one company has got inside another. The thing being reached for is rarely the whole business: it is a chip process, router source code, the control software for a wind turbine, a lease on a harbour, or the award of a contract at a state-owned utility. The most direct route is to buy the company outright, as the Shanghai-listed firm Wingtech did with the Dutch chipmaker Nexperia. The Dutch economy ministry took control of Nexperia's governance in 2025; China then blocked exports of chips packaged at its plant, and European carmakers ran short. The cheaper route is to hire the one engineer who already has the files, or to pay a manager inside a state power company for the inside track on contracts.

Where the buyer answers to a foreign state, the calculation changes, because a commercial decision becomes a government one. China's 2017 National Intelligence Law requires Chinese organisations to assist state intelligence when asked, which is why a Chinese owner of a port lease or a telecom supplier is treated differently from any other owner.

None of it goes to a vote. A board approves a sale, a territorial government signs a 99-year lease, an engineer copies files to a drive. It becomes visible through a criminal case, an export licence, a national-security review, or a shortage that reaches the factory floor years after the deal was done.
implications: Control over something people depend on every day, such as a power station contract, a phone network or the port their goods move through, can change hands without any public decision, and the bill arrives later. European carmakers stopped lines when Nexperia chips stopped coming. At a state utility, a bribed manager means the contract goes to the firm that paid, and the cost lands on electricity bills. Workers at the company whose designs were copied lose the orders those designs would have won. Worth watching: foreign purchases of chipmakers, ports and telecom suppliers, engineers moving between rival firms, and contracts at state-owned utilities and airlines.
uncertain: Several of these cases are unresolved or have gone the other way: Huawei's racketeering trial is under way, a US court acquitted Fujian Jinhua in the Micron case, and an Australian review found no security grounds to cancel the Port of Darwin lease. Whether a state-linked owner has ever actually been asked to act for its government, under China's intelligence law or otherwise, is not established in any of these records.

title: Spyware and elections for hire
summary: Running an election is a service that can be bought from abroad, and the trade continues even where the best-known brand names have closed. What is on offer is a package: polling and voter targeting, a party's rebranding and sometimes its manifesto, networks of fake accounts to push a message or discredit an opponent, and hacking of a rival campaign's phones and accounts. The buyer is a candidate or a government with money, and the work is bought the way any consultancy is bought, through a contract for data or branding paid out of campaign funds, which is why it rarely looks unusual in the accounts. Cambridge Analytica, a British political-data firm that closed in 2018, had its managing director filmed saying it ran two winning presidential campaigns in Kenya, rebranded the party twice and wrote its manifesto. Beside this sits the surveillance trade. Phone spyware such as Pegasus is licensed to governments only, and once a government holds it, it can be aimed at another country's politicians and officers: Morocco was named as having selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones as targets, which it denies. Russian political strategists have worked several African presidential races and sent people to watch a vote under the name of an independent monitoring body. The voter sees local-looking posts and independent-looking observers, and none of the contracts behind them.
implications: What reaches a voter is shaped by people they will never identify. The accounts arguing in their language are rented, the observers who vouch for the count were recruited by one side, and the opposition candidate's phone may be readable by whoever paid for the tool. Bans and blacklists do little, because the staff move on and set up again under a new name. Things to watch: data or consulting lines in campaign spending that nobody can explain, clusters of new accounts appearing in the weeks before a vote, observer missions with no record behind them, and spyware found on the phones of serving ministers.
uncertain: A great deal of this rests on undercover recordings and on the operators' own sales claims, including one contractor's claim of work on 33 presidential elections, which was never tested. Governments named as spyware clients deny it. Spain said its prime minister's phone was infected but did not establish who did it, and the court case was shelved.

title: Scam compounds and casino money inside Asian states
summary: Two governments in Southeast Asia are now prosecuting or dismantling businesses that had reached inside them. The business is online fraud and gambling run out of guarded compounds, and it needs three things the state controls: a licence, local officials who do not look too closely, and a bank or payment firm willing to move the proceeds. In the Philippines the licence came from the state gaming regulator, which authorised Chinese-run offshore gambling operators to serve players inside China; Senate hearings tied many of them to fraud, trafficking and torture. A town mayor there, found by a court to be a Chinese citizen rather than the Filipina she claimed to be, is serving life for trafficking, a former presidential spokesman faces warrants over another compound, and the industry is now banned by statute. In Cambodia the reach went to the top of the government rather than to a town hall. The head of one of the country's largest conglomerates held an honorary title and advised the former prime minister, the interior minister and the National Assembly president while, US prosecutors say, running an empire of scam compounds; US authorities seized about 127,271 bitcoin from him, and Cambodia has since revoked his citizenship and sent him to China. A Phnom Penh payment firm with the current prime minister's cousin as a director lost its banking licence after US regulators called the group a laundering hub.
implications: The people inside the compounds are the ones trafficked into them, often on a false job offer, and they cannot walk out past guards who have no reason to fear the local police. The victims are elsewhere, defrauded by phone and app, with little chance of getting anything back. Neighbours may see only a new walled complex and a generous local donor. What to watch: whether the Philippine ban holds once attention moves on, whether any official at home is investigated over the Cambodian cases, and which banks keep handling the payments.
uncertain: The Cambodian conglomerate case rests on a US indictment; its subject was sent to China rather than tried in Cambodia or the United States, and no Cambodian official has been charged. The former Philippine spokesman denies acting for the compound operator and has sought asylum abroad. How far either government's own officials were involved is not established on the record.

title: Iran's armed allies inside governments
roles: Where they sit in the state
summary:
In Lebanon and Iraq, armed movements backed by Iran hold office inside the states whose armies they sit outside — openly, with ministries, parliamentary seats and brigades paid from the national budget. Nothing here is covert, which makes it the plainest arrangement on the map and the hardest to undo.

The ministries involved are the ones that hand out jobs, money and services. In Lebanon, Hezbollah — a Shia party with its own armed wing, listed as a terrorist organisation by many governments including the United States and Britain — has its picks running health and labour, and with its ally Amal holds six of the twenty-four portfolios in the government formed in February 2025. In Iraq the route was legislation. The Popular Mobilization Forces, a body of mostly Shia factions raised in 2014 to fight Islamic State and almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, were written into the armed forces by a law passed two years later, placed under the prime minister and put on the state payroll. One faction inside it that the United States lists as a terrorist group staffs several of its brigades, and the PMF's own chief of staff has said it takes orders from Iran's supreme leader.

Further out the same network appears smaller and less formal: traders and financiers close to presidents in West Africa and South America, men tried in Kenya over explosives. What it gives Tehran is a voice at another state's cabinet table and armed units that another state's taxpayers fund.
implications: People pay taxes that fund brigades whose own commanders say they answer in part to a government abroad, and decisions that can start a war get taken outside the cabinet supposed to make them. The ministries in question are the ones that approve a hospital's drugs or a public-sector job, so patronage follows the party rather than the citizen. Disarmament is agreed in principle and left without a date. Worth watching: whether a timetable appears, whether bills to bring state-funded militias under government control actually pass, and who holds the ministries that distribute services.
uncertain: Several entries rest on US sanctions designations, which are one government's judgement rather than a court's finding and can be withdrawn — the designation of a former Paraguayan president was lifted in 2025. The dossier records a PMF commander's own statement about taking orders from Iran's supreme leader, but does not establish a chain of command on the ground.

title: Private forums where officials meet money
summary:
A large share of the people running Western governments also belong to a handful of private clubs, conferences and networks, and most of it is on the record: the attendance lists are published and the membership is lawful. What is not published is the conversation. The Bilderberg Meeting brings about 130 politicians, executives, bankers and military commanders together once a year under a rule that nothing said is attributable, and sitting prime ministers, presidents, European Commissioners and regional military commanders appear on its lists. The World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme works more slowly: it selects people under about 40 each year, among them serving ministers and prime ministers, and keeps them in a network of meetings and courses for years afterwards.

In the United States some of these bodies supply the work rather than just the room. The American Legislative Exchange Council has state legislators and corporate members draft model bills side by side, which then arrive in statehouses as ordinary legislation. The Federalist Society, a network of conservative lawyers, supplies the lists from which judges are chosen. The Heritage Foundation wrote a governing plan whose chapter authors now hold the posts their chapters describe.

What members get is each other. The official who will decide a bank rule, a defence contract or a judgeship spends days in the same building as the people affected, with no minutes kept, and the same circle reconvenes under the next government. What is missing is everyone without a seat, and any record of what was said.
uncertain: Membership and office are both documented; influence is not. No inquiry has found that any of these forums directed a member's decisions in office, and the record attaches that caveat to the long-serving Mont Pelerin Society members who held finance and foreign ministries. Because the meetings are held off the record, neither the claim of influence nor the denial can be tested.

implications: A bill can reach a state legislature already written, with the company that benefits having helped draft it, and the representative introducing it under no duty to say where it came from. Judges can be picked from a list assembled by a private network of lawyers. A minister who will rule on a merger or a contract spends three days with the people it affects and keeps no note of it. Worth watching: which of your ministers appear on each year's published attendance list, whether a bill in your state matches a published model bill, and who wrote the plan a new administration is working through.

summary: Bodies that cross borders, in policing, health, sport, justice and the European Parliament, are meant to answer to all their members and to none of them in particular, and several are now dealing with outsiders inside. What a government or a company wins here is larger than a national decision: who appears on the worldwide wanted list, which diseases get funded, what a climate text says, which country hosts a tournament. The targets are correspondingly narrow, because leadership of these bodies is settled by a few hundred votes and their committees by a few dozen, which makes a campaign for a presidency cheap next to the power of the office. Money arrives mostly as voluntary donations rather than membership dues, and a donor can earmark what its money does: the Gates Foundation, a private US charity, was the World Health Organization's second-largest funder and directs most of what it gives to programmes it chooses. The cruder approaches are familiar from national politics. In Brussels, prosecutors allege that cash, travel and football tickets reached members of the European Parliament on behalf of Qatar, Morocco and a Chinese telecoms company, which those accused deny. The people who pay for all this are not in the room: a refugee can be held at an airport in a third country on an alert filed by the government he fled.
uncertain: The Brussels cases are still at investigation or trial, the people charged deny wrongdoing, and an appeal court has allowed the Qatargate prosecution to go ahead rather than resolved it. Allegations of pressure and inducements on delegations voting for a UN agency's leadership were reported but not tested. The World Bank inquiry found that leaders pressed staff to change a country's ranking, which is not the same as a finding that anything was paid for it.

A health budget goes to the illnesses a donor picked rather than the ones killing most people where the money lands. A climate summit is chaired by a man who also runs a state oil company, with talking points for his government meetings drafted by that company. Worth watching: large voluntary gifts in the months before an election for a top post, officials moving straight from a national ministry into the body meant to check it, and how a parliament votes on lifting its own members' immunity.

title: Movements that sought the state itself

countries.note: A military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors in 2012 of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir.
The army said in January 2012 it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir.

summary: Right now these movements are being pushed out of governments they once helped run, by designation rather than by votes. The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 with branches across the region, mostly did not infiltrate anything: it stood for election, and won. Its candidate took Egypt's presidency and the army removed him a year later. Parties in the same tradition led the governments of Tunisia and Morocco for years, and a Brotherhood-linked party is still the largest in Jordan's parliament with 31 of 138 seats. What has changed is the legal status of the parent movement. Jordan banned all its activities in April 2025 while that party kept its seats, and in January 2026 the United States designated the Egyptian, Jordanian and Lebanese branches as terrorist bodies for the first time. Egypt has outlawed the group since the coup that removed its president, and several Gulf states list it. Tunisia's former speaker of parliament, who led the party that governed after the 2011 uprising, is serving long sentences his party calls political. A second movement, Hizb ut-Tahrir, refuses elections altogether and calls for a single caliphate; in two countries it went for the army instead. A Pakistani military court convicted a brigadier and four majors of links to it, and Bangladesh's army named it over a coup plot it says it stopped. Britain has made membership a crime.
uncertain: Where these movements won office they did so in the open, and the dossier records no finding that they entered the state by deception. The infiltration claim has not always held up: Austria's 2020 raids on suspected Brotherhood networks were ruled unlawful, and a 2025 French state report that warned of Brotherhood 'entryism' at municipal level also found no recent document showing a wish to set up an Islamic state in France. Several of the Tunisian and Egyptian convictions are contested as politically driven.

confirmed_by.title: Egyptian cabinet designation, 25 December 2013
Pakistan Army field general court martial, August 2012

implications: A ban on a movement does not stop at the movement. It reaches the party that grew out of it and the people who voted for that party, who find the largest bloc in their parliament attached to an outlawed organisation. Charities, schools and clinics run by members can be closed and their assets seized. The label travels: once a government calls a current of politics infiltration, prosecutions of its politicians become hard to tell apart from ordinary cases against the opposition. Watch whether courts review the bans, and what happens to the seats at the next election.

title: Lodges inside police forces and courts
summary:
Officers and staff of London's Metropolitan Police now have to declare whether they are Freemasons. The governing body of English Freemasonry went to the High Court to stop the rule and lost, a judge calling it a proportionate way of protecting public trust in policing. The argument is about disclosure, not about wrongdoing: belonging to a lawful fraternity is not an offence.

It matters in these particular jobs because a police officer or a judge is meant to owe loyalty to the law alone, and someone who is arrested or tried cannot see whether the officer or the judge shares a private obligation with the other side. The record mainly shows how hard that is to check. A Commons committee in the 1990s said it obtained the Grand Lodge's cooperation only 'through compulsion' after months of prevarication, and the Grand Lodge needed five attempts to produce a list of masons in one disbanded police squad. A declaration rule was introduced for new judges and police in 1998 and dropped for judges in 2009, after a review found no evidence of impropriety.

Where the secrecy was complete, the damage was larger. Italy learned who sat in the Propaganda Due lodge only because officers searching a factory for something else found the membership list, and on it were the heads of all three intelligence services and the commander of the financial police. A 1982 law banning secret associations that interfere with public bodies has been used since, in the P3 case, against a later network.
uncertain: Nothing here establishes that a lodge, as an organisation, directed a police force or a court; what is documented is overlapping membership, obstruction of inquiries, and in Italy a list seized by chance. The 2009 review of English judges found masonic membership among a small share of them and no evidence of impropriety. Some entries, such as reports naming Romanian ministers and a Gabonese police chief, rest on press accounts citing masonic sources and have never been tested.

confirmed_by.title: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, Freemasonry in the Police and the Judiciary, 1997; Freemasonry in Public Life, 1999
Italian Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission, report on Freemasonry, December 2017

implications: If you are arrested, charged or sued, you cannot tell whether the officer, prosecutor or judge in your case is bound by a private obligation to someone on the other side, and where no register exists neither can the force or the court. In one 1988 assault at a lodge function attended mostly by serving officers, it was the two men who were assaulted who ended up charged; they were acquitted and the force paid most of the settlement. Worth watching: whether forces besides the Met adopt a declaration rule, what happens to memberships that go undeclared, and whether judges are brought back under a register.

title: French lodges and African presidencies
roles: Head of state or minister in a lodge
case_role: Head of state or minister in a lodge

countries.note: The Grande Loge Nationale Française and the Grand Orient de France sponsored or chartered lodges in former colonies; the GLNF's grand master installed Ali Bongo as grand master of Gabon's lodge in 2009. Jacques Foccart's Service d'Action Civique ran France's African networks from the Élysée.

summary:
In a dozen former French colonies, Masonic lodges sponsored from Paris still sit next to the presidency. The two large French bodies, the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française, charter or affiliate national lodges in Africa, and in several countries the grand mastership of that lodge has travelled with the office of head of state: a president founds the lodge, leads it for decades, and his successor is installed in the post by a visiting French grand master. Ministers, police commanders and state prosecutors turn up in the same rooms. In Gabon, where the grand mastership traditionally went to the president, it passed to a provincial governor after the 2023 coup, and the head of the Grand Orient reportedly met the coup leader in Libreville soon afterwards and offered support.

None of this is unlawful, and belonging to a lodge is not wrongdoing. What the arrangement provides is a private and durable meeting place that cuts across a government and across a border, where a French Masonic official and an African president can talk with no agenda, no minute and no parliament told. It outlasts changes of government, because the lodge is not part of the state.

The French roots are older than the African ones, and they show what the structure can do once it reaches inside an institution: between 1901 and 1904 the French War Ministry used reports gathered through Grand Orient lodges to sort army officers for promotion by religion and politics, and when it came out the government fell.
uncertain: Most of the African memberships rest on press reporting, chiefly a 2012 Jeune Afrique survey, rather than on lodge records; some are denied, and in several cases no lodge is named. The record does not establish that any decision of state was taken inside a lodge.

confirmed_by.title: Jeune Afrique, investigation of Freemasonry in Africa, 2012
Le Monde, 1999, on payments to the Ordre Souverain du Temple Initiatique

implications: A citizen cannot easily tell that the president, the police commander and the prosecutor who might investigate them meet privately and regularly, or that the body chartering their lodge sits in another country. Appointments and business arranged in that room leave no record, so there is nothing to appeal against and nothing to vote on. After a coup or an election, among the first people to reach the new leader may be someone no one elected, from abroad. Worth watching: whether grand masterships still pass with the presidency, who visits a new leader in the weeks after a takeover, and whether any lodge publishes its officers.

title: Banks and banking families
summary: Banks reach governments today mostly through people moving between them, and nearly all of it is lawful and on the public record. The offices that matter are the ones that set the price of money and the rules banks live under: the finance ministry, the central bank, the agency that manages public debt, the regulator. Argentina's economy ministry and central bank are both run by former JPMorgan bankers, and Canada's prime minister worked at Goldman Sachs before heading two central banks. The traffic runs the other way too, with a former European Commission president going on to chair Goldman Sachs International, and governors meet privately every two months at the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, the central banks' own bank, whose Basel Committee drafts rules that national regulators then adopt. A second route is ownership: where politicians own the banks, as a study found for 18 of Lebanon's 20 major banks before the 2019 collapse, the state's debt and the owners' balance sheets become one problem. A third is lending a government money it keeps off the books, which is how Mozambique's borrowing for fishing and maritime security stayed hidden from its own parliament. Claims that a Jewish banking family secretly owns the US central bank or financed revolutions are antisemitic conspiracy theories; the Federal Reserve's board is nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, and one such family bank's records show it refused the Bolsheviks money.
implications: When a bank is in trouble, the people deciding how much public money it receives, and on what terms, often came out of banking and may return to it. A tax claim can lapse after a banker's meetings with a mayor. Rules agreed in a closed meeting in Basel become the law your own bank follows. And where politicians own the banks, savers lose their deposits while the owners' losses turn into the state's debt. Worth watching: who is appointed to run finance ministries and central banks, which firms are hired to advise on debt and privatisation, and whether a government's borrowing is shown to its parliament.
uncertain: The historian Carroll Quigley's account of bankers aiming at a world system of financial control in private hands is his own reading; he later wrote that they had great influence but not control of political life, and said he never called it a conspiracy. Several cases here are unfinished or ended without a conviction, including a Portuguese prime minister still on trial and a bank president acquitted. No inquiry has found a hidden body directing governments, and the movements described above are mostly open appointments.

title: Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network

summary: This is where a present-day habit comes from: filling the offices in which foreign policy is written from a very small circle. It begins with Cecil Rhodes, premier of the Cape Colony, who lost that post in 1896 after a failed armed incursion into the Boer Transvaal and whose wills left his fortune to extending British rule. Alfred Milner, sent out as High Commissioner, recruited young Oxford graduates into the government of the conquered Boer territories; that group, the Kindergarten, pressed for the Union of South Africa and founded the Round Table movement, with a journal and branches across the dominions. What followed is on the public record. Milner joined the five-man War Cabinet. The Round Table's first editor became the prime minister's private secretary and later ambassador to Washington. Milner's old secretary edited The Times through the appeasement years and wrote privately that he spent his nights taking out anything likely to hurt German opinion. At the Paris peace conference another of them convened British and American experts, who went home and founded Chatham House in London and the Council on Foreign Relations in New York; the Council then ran confidential postwar planning for the State Department on Rockefeller money. All of these were appointments made through normal channels, filled for about half a century by a few hundred men from the same colleges, the same colonial administration and the same clubs. The practice carries forward: an election still decides the party in office while a narrower set of institutes and private offices supplies the briefings its ministers read.
uncertain: The offices, committees and institutes here are documented; the existence of a formal secret society behind them rests on the account of one historian, Carroll Quigley, who said he read the group's papers, which is why many entries are marked only as possible. From 1970 other writers recast his network as a world conspiracy directed by bankers, a reading Quigley himself rejected and one the record of ordinary appointments does not support; claims of that kind about banking families have no evidentiary basis.

implications: Voters chose a party, and the papers its ministers read were often drafted inside the same circle — and so were the terms of a postwar settlement, the constitution of a colony, the line a national newspaper took on a foreign government. People in the territories affected had no part in it: a boundary commission that satisfied neither side, a scheme of partial self-rule for India, a union of four colonies. The use of this today is a habit of looking past the election result to the appointments — who becomes a private secretary, who runs the institute that briefs the ministry, and who pays for it.

title: The anticommunist web, 1945–1990

countries.note: Gladio, disclosed by Prime Minister Andreotti on 24 October 1990, and P2, whose 1981 list held the heads of all three intelligence services. Italy is where the stay-behind and lodge networks overlapped most.
The Chilean intelligence service DINA under Manuel Contreras called the founding meeting of Operation Condor in Santiago in November 1975.
CIA support for the stay-behind networks is confirmed in the Italian and Belgian inquiries; Condor's 1976 bombing of Orlando Letelier in Washington was carried out by DINA agents.

summary:
Much of what this map shows today grew out of a web of secret armies, lodges and intelligence clubs built after 1945 to fight communism. On paper the design was defensive. NATO, the Western military alliance, coordinated 'stay-behind' networks of officers and civilians in member countries, with hidden arms caches, who were to resist a Soviet invasion that never came. Parliaments were not told. Italy's network, Gladio, became public only in 1990, when the prime minister told the Chamber of Deputies it had existed since the 1950s; within months other governments admitted or began investigating their own. Switzerland's was funded outside parliament's control, and the full report on it stays sealed until 2041.

Around these networks grew others staffed by the same officers and intelligence men, and their work turned inward. The list seized from the head of Italy's Propaganda Due lodge in 1981 held 962 names, among them the heads of all three Italian intelligence services; in Argentina its members included a junta admiral and the minister whose ministry funded a death squad. From 1975 the secret police of several South American dictatorships ran Operation Condor to hunt each other's exiles across borders, including by car bomb in Washington.

None of it is finished. A Rome appeals court passed life sentences in the Condor case in 2019, and in 2025 Italy's highest court made final a verdict calling the head of P2 the knowing financier of the 1980 bombing of Bologna's railway station. Sealed files and pending verdicts are the normal condition of this history.
uncertain: Membership lists and parliamentary findings are firmer here than the claim that the stay-behind networks themselves carried out attacks at home; that link is disputed and, where it has been tested, has sometimes failed — Rome courts acquitted the head of P2 and others of conspiring against the state. Several of the Condor life sentences were passed in absentia. What individual stay-behind members were actually asked to do, as against what their networks stored, is largely not established on this record.

confirmed_by.title: European Parliament resolution on Gladio, 22 November 1990
Belgian Senate parliamentary inquiry on stay-behind networks, 1991
US National Security Archive, Operation Condor briefing books

implications: These were bodies set up for an emergency and kept long after it, outside the knowledge of the parliaments that paid for them, and the people they were eventually used against were at home: exiles, dissidents, protesters, and the passengers in a railway station. Citizens in the countries involved found out decades later, and usually only because a government changed, a parliament forced an inquiry, or files turned up by accident in a police station. Worth watching: which records remain sealed and until when, which courts are still ruling on the 1970s and 1980s, and who is made answerable for new emergency bodies.

countries.role: Where officials were paid or deposits lost
countries.note: BCCI secretly owned First American Bankshares in Washington through nominees; former Defense Secretary Clark Clifford, its chairman, was indicted in 1992 (charges dropped for ill health). The CIA held accounts at BCCI.

summary:
This is where today's arrangements for moving money quietly come from. In the 1970s and 1980s a few banks grew very large because a particular kind of customer, including a church, intelligence services, a dictator and an oil-state ruling family, needed money moved without questions, and a bank serving those customers is slow to be closed.

The shape repeats. The bank is licensed and supervised like any other. Its real owners sit behind nominees and offshore companies, so the regulator approving a takeover is looking at a front man. Its clients include states themselves: central bank reserves, a government's foreign-currency accounts, an army's payroll account. And the people who could act against it are using it. Banco Ambrosiano in Milan was Italy's largest private bank; its chairman belonged to P2, a secret lodge whose membership list, when financial police found it, named members of parliament, hundreds of military officers and the heads of all three Italian intelligence services. Italy's central bank had flagged the bank four years before it collapsed with about $1.3 billion unaccounted for.

Depositors and creditors lose their money, and a country that parked reserves there loses public funds. The officials who used the bank are mostly not convicted; some were shielded by a treaty, a plea bargain, or age and ill health. The thread runs into the present at the Vatican, whose own tribunal convicted a former head of its bank of embezzlement, and where a cardinal's conviction over a London property deal was annulled in 2026 with a retrial ordered.
uncertain: How Roberto Calvi died is still unsettled: one London inquest returned suicide, a second returned an open verdict, and a forensic report for an Italian court concluded murder. The Vatican Bank denied legal liability for Banco Ambrosiano while paying creditors $224 million. In the BCCI case the charges against Clark Clifford were dropped on grounds of age and health rather than tested, and his partner was acquitted.

confirmed_by.title: US Senate, The BCCI Affair (Kerry–Brown report), 1992
Bank of Italy inquiry into Banco Ambrosiano, 1981–82
Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking (Stewart), 1983–85

implications: When a bank like this fails, the loss does not land on the clients it was built to protect. Ordinary depositors and creditor banks write off what they had in it, and a country whose central bank placed reserves there loses public money that the budget then has to absorb: Peru had $270 million sitting at BCCI's Panama branch. The clients, meanwhile, move on, because a bank of that kind is replaced before anyone closes it. Worth watching: which banks hold government accounts and central bank reserves, and how long a supervisor's warning sits in a drawer before anything is done about it.

title: Sworn brotherhoods that chose who governed

countries.note: Every prime minister and state president from D. F. Malan (1948) to F. W. de Klerk (1989–94) was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918. Its membership list was published by journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom in 1978.

Army officers who later founded the Black Hand killed King Alexander Obrenović in 1903 and its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis', became head of military intelligence; its rival, the White Hand, put General Petar Živković in power as prime minister in 1929.
IDEA, a secret society of army officers, prepared the April 1967 coup; the colonels ruled until 1974 and were tried in 1975.

The Society of St. Tammany ran New York City's Democratic machine; the Know Nothings won Massachusetts in 1854; the 1920s Klan elected governors in Indiana, Colorado and Oregon and helped send Hugo Black to the Senate and then the Supreme Court.

summary: This is the older form that the arrangements elsewhere on the map grew out of: in some countries a sworn society did not slip people into a government, it decided who formed one. Two things make it work, a closed membership and an office worth holding. In South Africa the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society, counted every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 among its members, and a 1979 report found that all but two cabinet ministers belonged, along with the heads of the army and of state security and dozens of people inside the state broadcaster. In the Balkans the societies were made of army officers, who used the lever officers have: Serbian officers killed their king, and their leader was afterwards made chief of military intelligence. In North America the lodges built city and state machines, with a sworn nativist order taking a state governorship and nearly its whole legislature in the 1850s, and Orangemen holding the Toronto mayoralty for most of a century. What these brotherhoods wanted was not a contract but the composition of the state itself: who could be a judge, a teacher, a police chief, a citizen. The cost fell on everyone outside a membership defined by race, religion or sex. It has not entirely passed. An FBI inquiry found in 2014 that a deputy police chief and an officer in a small Florida town had been involved with the Ku Klux Klan.
uncertain: Membership of most of these societies was secret, so much of the record comes from later journalism, leaks and testimony, and many entries are marked probable or possible rather than established. Some endorsements, such as the Klan's backing of particular governors, were secret at the time and surfaced only years later. Carroll Quigley's account of a secret society around Cecil Rhodes and Alfred Milner is his reading of the papers; the offices those men held are documented, the society's direction of them is not.

confirmed_by.title: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)
Greek junta trials, 1975
Indiana and Colorado Klan histories; Hugo Black's radio address, 1 October 1937

implications: Where one society picks the candidates, an election decides only which of its members holds the office. For 46 years, South Africans who were not white Afrikaner men had no way into the body that chose their rulers, so voting changed nothing about who they were choosing between. Nothing looks irregular from outside, because the members are the government: there is no bribe to trace and no outside lobbyist to register. What to watch for is overlap, the same private membership turning up at once among ministers, police commanders, judges and broadcasters, and officers policing people their society will not admit.

summary: This is the origin of an argument governments are still having: who pays for the civic groups that work across borders. In the early Cold War the CIA, the United States' foreign intelligence service, quietly paid for a set of bodies that presented themselves as private and independent. The choice of bodies was consistent. The money went not to governments but to the places where opinion is formed and organised: a cultural congress with offices in dozens of countries and its own literary magazines, the federation of American college student governments, radio stations broadcasting into the Soviet bloc, a foundation working across Asia that an internal CIA memorandum described as a Central Intelligence Agency proprietary. It moved through private foundations so that a grant looked philanthropic; the Senate's Church Committee later found CIA money in at least 108 of 700 large grants made by 164 US foundations over a four-year period. It also reached other countries' elections, through an American union committee in Italy and through a Brazilian institute that paid for opposition campaigns. The people reading the magazines and attending the conferences were not told. From 1983 much of this work moved into the open, into an endowment funded by Congress whose own founder said that a lot of what it did had been done covertly by the CIA twenty-five years earlier. The secret period is what carries into the present: it gives any government a ready reason to treat a foreign-funded group as a front, and Russia and China have both banned that endowment on exactly that argument.
uncertain: Some entries are claims rather than findings: the labour institute's trainees being 'intimately involved' in Brazil's 1964 coup comes from its own director's later remark, and the extent of CIA involvement in the 1962 Brazilian elections was examined by a parliamentary inquiry rather than settled by a court. The Russian and Chinese designations of the National Endowment for Democracy are political acts, not evidence that it operates covertly.
