implications: A reader of a literary magazine, a student delegate at a conference, a voter in an election where one side's campaign was quietly paid for from abroad — none of them knew, and that is the cost: they could not weigh what they were being told. The effect outlasts the funding. A government that wants to close a human rights group or a newspaper can point to this history and call foreign money a front, and groups funded openly and lawfully pay for it. The practical question about any civic body, magazine or broadcaster is who pays and whether that is published.

title: Lenders, aid programmes and trained technocrats
roles: Country whose economy was run by the trainees or advisers
case_role: Country whose economy was run by the trainees or advisers

countries.note: The Ford Foundation paid for Indonesian economists to train at Berkeley; the US aid agency (ICA, later USAID) funded the 1956 agreement between the University of Chicago and Chile's Catholic University; the US Treasury ran the Saudi Joint Commission from a Saudi-funded trust account.

timeline.event: Chile Project links University of Chicago and Catholic University of Chile under US aid

summary:
This is where a pattern that still runs through international lending begins: a country's economic ministries staffed by people trained, funded or advised through another country's programmes, with nothing covert about it at any stage. In the late 1950s the Ford Foundation, an American philanthropy, paid for University of Indonesia economists to take doctorates at Berkeley. When Suharto took power in 1966 they became his economic team; one ran the national planning agency and another was finance minister — the post that decides who gets the state's money — each for about fifteen years. In Chile a US aid scheme begun in 1955 and later carried on by the same foundation linked Santiago's Catholic University to the University of Chicago. Its graduates wrote the plan that became the junta's economic programme, then took the finance, economy and planning ministries and the central bank.

The mechanism is simple and lawful. Train the officials, or pay the advisers who sit beside them, and the policy follows without anyone having to ask for it. Saudi Arabia's version was a joint commission set up in 1974 and co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary, which supplied American advisers paid out of a Saudi account held at the Treasury; a US government audit found it recycled oil money into American goods and services.

The debts contracted in those years were left to later governments to repay, and the conditions lenders attach to loans carry the same logic into the present.
uncertain: The link documented here is training and funding, not instruction: the record does not show these ministers taking orders from the programmes that educated them. The claim that an American engineering firm's chief economist was employed to inflate growth forecasts so that countries would borrow comes from his own 2004 book; a newspaper investigation found his career accurately described but no evidence of the intelligence recruitment he alleged, and the State Department called much of the account fabricated.

confirmed_by.title: US General Accounting Office report on the US–Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation, 1979
New York Times, 'Economic Hit Man' review, 2005

implications: Decisions that reshape daily life — selling off state firms, opening the economy to foreign capital, borrowing heavily for large projects — get made by ministers nobody in the country elected, and in Indonesia and Chile they served military governments. The bill arrived later: the loans had to be repaid by governments and taxpayers who had no part in taking them on. What someone can look for now is who trained a country's finance and central-bank officials, who pays its foreign advisers, and which outside lender sets the conditions on its budget.

title: Exposure, purge and reversal

timeline.event: US Senate Church Committee begins hearings on intelligence abuses
Italian police find the P2 list at Licio Gelli's villa (17 March)
Andreotti discloses Gladio to the Italian parliament (24 October)
Regulators in seven countries close BCCI (5 July)
Paraguay's 'Archives of Terror' found in Lambaré (22 December)

summary:
This is where the shape of today's infiltration cases comes from: nearly all of them sit somewhere in a cycle that has been repeating for a century, and knowing which part explains how much of a story has actually been tested.

Exposure comes first, and almost never from the body meant to be watching. It comes from a search in an unrelated case, a car crash, a leak, a defection or a change of government. In 1981 Italian financial police investigating a different banker searched a factory and came out with a membership list for a secret lodge holding 962 names, among them members of parliament, hundreds of military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services.

Then comes the purge. A government bans the organisation, often under a law written for the occasion, and removes the people it says belong to it. The removals are administrative, done by decree or by a judicial council rather than by trial, so they run far wider than the evidence would carry: judges, police, soldiers and teachers dismissed in their thousands, and companies handed to a state trustee.

Years later the courts narrow it. Convictions are quashed for want of evidence that the organisation existed at all, defendants are acquitted when the documents turn out to be forged, and some of the people removed in the purge are reinstated while others, removed on the same basis, are not. The cycle is still running, which is why a present-day case on this map can look settled and then move.
uncertain: The cycle describes how these cases move, not whether the underlying claims are true; in several of them a court's finding and a government's account still contradict each other. Reversals cut both ways: the Sledgehammer acquittals followed a finding that the evidence had been forged, while other reversals came with no explanation on the record. Which reversals corrected a mistake and which were political is not established here.

confirmed_by.title: Italian Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982
Turkish Constitutional Court and Court of Cassation rulings on Ergenekon and Sledgehammer, 2015–16

implications: In a purge, people lose their jobs by decree rather than at a hearing: judges removed in a day, police and soldiers dismissed in their thousands, businesses handed to a state trustee fund. Years later a court may restore some of them and not others on the same evidence, and from outside the two groups look identical. For anyone reading a story like this, the useful questions are which stage it has reached, who exposed it and why at that moment, and whether any of it has been tested in court. A sanctions listing, a parliamentary finding and a conviction are three different things.
